subject: Business Studies
name: Business Studies, Year 11: Management and planning
syllabus: NSW Business Studies Stage 6 Syllabus (2010), Year 11 course, Business management and Business planning topics

points.title: What managers do
points.brief: Managers plan, organise, lead and control the work of a business so it meets its goals. Each role links to the others.

points.title: Management skills
points.brief: Good managers need interpersonal skills, communication, decision-making, problem-solving and the ability to plan ahead and adapt.

points.title: Stakeholders
points.brief: People with an interest in a business, such as owners, employees, customers, suppliers, the government and the community. Their interests often conflict.

points.title: Corporate social responsibility
points.brief: A business acting for the good of society and the environment beyond what the law requires, such as cutting waste or treating suppliers fairly.

points.title: Management and the triple bottom line
points.brief: Judging a business on its financial, social and environmental results, not on profit alone.

points.title: The classical scientific approach
points.brief: Frederick Taylor broke work into simple, measured tasks, with workers paid for output. It raised productivity but treated workers like parts of a machine.

points.title: The classical bureaucratic approach
points.brief: Clear hierarchy, written rules, set roles and authority from the top, drawing on Max Weber and Henri Fayol. It brings order but can be slow and rigid.

points.title: The behavioural approach
points.brief: Elton Mayo's Hawthorne studies suggested that attention, teamwork and meeting social needs lift motivation. Managers lead and consult rather than only command.

points.title: The political approach
points.brief: Businesses are made of groups with different interests competing for power and resources. Managers negotiate and build alliances.

points.title: The systems approach
points.brief: A business is a system of connected parts that takes in inputs, transforms them and produces outputs, and must keep adapting to its environment.

points.title: The contingency approach
points.brief: There is no single best way to manage. The right approach depends on the situation, so managers adapt their style to the problem in front of them.

points.title: Forces for change
points.brief: External forces, such as new technology, competition and law, and internal forces, such as a new manager or poor results, push a business to change.

points.title: Resistance to change
points.brief: People resist change because of costs, fear of the unknown, lost status, habit and poor communication.

points.title: Managing change well
points.brief: Explaining the need for change, involving staff, setting clear goals, training and supporting people through it make change more likely to succeed.

points.title: Force field analysis
points.brief: Kurt Lewin's model lists forces driving change and forces resisting it. Change happens when the driving forces outweigh the restraining ones.

chapters.title: Starting a small to medium enterprise

points.title: The decision to start a business
points.brief: People start businesses to be their own boss, follow an idea or earn more. Before starting, they weigh their skills, money and the risk.

points.title: Market research for a new business
points.brief: Finding out who the customers are, what they want, what competitors offer and whether enough people will buy, before spending money.

points.title: Choosing a location
points.brief: Location affects costs and sales. Owners weigh access to customers, suppliers and staff, rent, visibility and competitors nearby.

points.title: Financing a new business
points.brief: Money to start can come from the owner's savings (equity) or loans (debt). Equity keeps control but risks the owner's money. Debt must be repaid with interest.

points.title: Resources needed to start
points.brief: A new business needs premises, equipment, stock, staff and systems such as accounts. Planning these in advance avoids running short.

points.title: Why a business plan matters
points.brief: A business plan sets out goals and how to reach them. It guides decisions and is used to win finance from lenders and investors.

points.title: Vision, mission and goals
points.brief: The vision is what the business wants to become, the mission is its purpose, and goals are measurable targets that put them into action.

points.title: SWOT analysis
points.brief: Listing internal strengths and weaknesses and external opportunities and threats, to plan around what the business can control and what it cannot.

points.title: Parts of a business plan
points.brief: A plan covers marketing, operations, finance and human resources, each with its own goals and actions.

points.title: Levels of planning
points.brief: Strategic plans cover several years for the whole business, tactical plans one to two years for a part of it, and operational plans the day-to-day.

points.title: Monitoring performance
points.brief: Comparing actual results, such as sales or costs, with the plan and acting early when they fall short.

points.title: Benchmarking
points.brief: Comparing a business's performance with a standard, such as a competitor or industry average, to find ways to improve.

points.title: Contingency planning
points.brief: Planning ahead for what could go wrong, such as a supplier failing, so the business can respond quickly.

points.title: Why small businesses succeed or fail
points.brief: Good planning, enough money, sound management and knowing the customer help small businesses succeed. Cash flow problems and poor planning often cause failure.
